title: Revival
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin tells the story of how a girl from Wilmington, Ohio ended up as Eno at a Zen sangha in the Pacific Northwest, and what Nyogen loves in the Zen forms. Nyogen follows a pattern of turning away and turning toward: a revival tent preacher and the unwelcome treatment of two classmates at church, then a son, Nathaniel, born with severe disabilities. Anger brings Nyogen to practice and to Norman Fischer. At Nyogen's first retreat, eighty Great Blue Herons crossing a lagoon stop Nyogen's mind. Nyogen calls ritual alive, citing a Zhaozhou exchange on zazen, and ends with Nathaniel driving a John Deere tractor and playing in a rock band.

It's just so improbable that little Connie Sue Schaeffer from Wilmington, Ohio would come and end up in the Eno seat at a Buddhist Zen Sangha in the Pacific Northwest.
Especially end up being Eno in that Sangha, and especially end up sitting here giving a talk.
So I want to talk to you tonight about two things.
One is what brought me here.
I guess that's way-seeking mind, or maybe way-wandering mind, or confused seeking mind.
And the second thing I want to talk about is my love of the Zen forms, of the ritual that we do.
My way-seeking mind really seems confused, taking quite a few detours, going down some one-way streets and ending up at a lot of dead ends.
But there are a couple of things, a couple of patterns, that seem to have followed me throughout.
One has been turning away from things and the other has been turning toward things.
So it's a strange tale of fire and brimstone, Tarzan, betrayal, Princeton and publishing, Microsoft, which was a religion unto itself.
Not good enough.
A kid who can't talk.
Anger.
Anger.
Practice.
Great Blue Herons, Zoketsu, Zazen, Out of the Ashes and John Deere.
I won't try to cover all those things, but you'll get it when I hit a few of the highlights.
So the turning away has been turning away from pain, turning from difficulty, turning from reality.
And then slowly, gradually, learning that I can turn toward my life.
I can turn toward difficulty.
I can turn toward pain and not fall apart, or at least not totally fall apart.
Okay, let's start the tale.
Chapter two.
Tarzan.
I was probably about ten years old and I was reading my very first novel.
Tarzan wandered into a decaying temple deep in the African jungle and caught a whiff of incense.
Intermingled with the spore of the gorilla man was a sweet scent, burning incense, along with the spore of Numa the lion.
So I turned toward it and dreamt of going to Africa.
I knew there was more to the world than the corn and tomatoes that I found in Ohio.
I still love the smell of incense.
I still love corn and tomatoes.
And I have actually seen lions in the Masai Mara.
To back up for a moment, chapter one.
Fire and brimstone.
I'll get to the Zen part soon, but in the meantime, at another temple, great Uncle Sam, whose picture is back there on the table, or actually whose flyer is back there on the table.
A revival preacher with a Bible and a tent.
A real tent.
I remember this from when I was really young.
He stomped back and forth on the stage, shaking his fist, his voice hoarse as he shouted about sin and damnation, abomination in the eyes of the Lord.
The music was nice.
I can't really sing very well, but I do remember it.
*Come to the church in the wildwood.
Oh, come to the church in the lane.*
Still turning toward.
I attended Sunday school.
I taught vacation Bible class.
I studied the Bible and I even thought about becoming a missionary.
And please don't anyone tell Chris that.
I invited a couple of my classmates to come to Sunday school with me.
I don't really remember why I made that invitation.
I wasn't especially close to these two people, but we tended to hang out together sometimes in homeroom.
Those two girls were black and they did accept my invitation.
They came to church with me and they were treated with exquisite politeness.
And it was so clear that they were not welcome.
I knew that racism existed, but that was probably the first time that I had ever encountered it in such a direct way.
And I didn't do anything dramatic.
I didn't have the courage to confront the hypocrisy.
I just turned away.
If I'd been older or more mature, I might have realized that I would find hypocrisy in any religion.
But at age 13, that small event had a huge impact on me.
I was old enough to be passionate in my beliefs and to experience a deep feeling of betrayal.
I was not old enough to see what had happened in any kind of broader context.
But in the face of racism, I turned away.
I did not want anything more to do with religion.
And I turned away for a long, long time.
So that chapter ended.
Chapter three, and probably chapter four and five as well.
Living my life.
College, marriage, a career in publishing, print production designer at Microsoft.
Great dogs.
Really great dogs, and a pretty good life.
I thought for a long time that you just lived your life as well as you could.
You did your best.
You throw a ball for your dogs.
You invite friends for dinner.
You work hard and you don't forget to take a walk on the beach and smell the salt water.
I thought that it wasn't really possible to understand what life was really about in any big way.
I guess it was don't-know mind, but not really beginner's mind.
And in Dogen's term, it's probably the stage of mountains are mountains.
My husband wanted kids.
I wasn't so keen on the idea, but I balked partly because I had edited this college textbook called Medical Ethics.
And that book scared me badly.
Actually, it scared the shit out of me.
It was a lot of stuff about what can go wrong with the human body, especially what can go wrong with the tiny infant bodies of children.
Even before that, I knew that I'd never be one who would turn toward wanting to have a kid with special needs or a kid with serious medical problems.
But in spite of that, I took a leap of faith and I agreed that we'd try to get pregnant.
We couldn't get pregnant, so we turned toward adoption.
And we adopted our son, Nathaniel, when he was five days old.
As Lieutenant O'Hara once said to Captain Kirk, be careful what you wish for.
You may get it.
My mantra became, be careful what you wish not for.
You will get it.
I learned the meaning of the word perseverate.
I learned the meaning of proprioception.
I took Nathaniel to therapy.
I'm still learning to deal with serious behavioral problems.
Nathaniel is 24 years old, and he probably is anywhere between the age of four and 24, depending on what you ask of him.
He's pretty severely disabled, mostly mentally, not so much physically.
If you watched him walk across the room, you would know that something was wrong.
You might not know what.
He signs.
He hears, but he doesn't talk.
So he signs, but not fluently.
I learned to sign to him, to give him a way to communicate with other people.
Nathaniel gets frustrated and he may bang his head on the wall or on the ground if he's really unhappy.
He knows what he wants, and he wants it when he wants it.
And he makes it pretty clear when he's unhappy.
So it was relatively easy to deal with that in a four-year-old, not so much in a 24-year-old.
And yet sometimes Nathaniel is really sweet.
And I'm probably gonna have to ask someone to hand me some Kleenex.
He signs, love, mom.
And sometimes he tries so hard that it breaks my heart, and it was a good cry.

Probably most of you noticed the difficulty I had in listening to Andrea's talk about the woman whose child has died, and the Buddha sends her to look for a house in the town whose family has not suffered some kind of a loss.
And of course, she can't find anyone, and she comes to accept that her child has died.
With a child with a serious disability, it can be almost like that death happens over and over again, because it's the death of having your child talk to you.
It's the death of the idea of those first words.
It's the death of all of the benchmarks that are sort of normal with normal kids.
So that loss happens over and over again.
And you can't fix it.
It doesn't heal.
And it seems like it doesn't end.
Turning away under those conditions wasn't, for me, a choice.
I was, though, angry at the universe.
So I was given this terrible situation, and it was clear at a pretty young age that there were serious problems.
So I had this terrible situation.
I couldn't turn away, and I had to find a way to, if not embrace it, at least do something with it.
My marriage was falling apart.
And actually, that's not real unusual when there's a kid with a severe disability.
But my marriage was falling apart, and a question to a psychotherapist was answered in terms of her Zen practice.
Chapter six, entitled Practice and the Recurring Theme of Not Good Enough.
So it was the anger that brought me to practice.
I read a couple of books, Stephen Batchelor's Buddhism Without Beliefs, which I still recommend highly, and Charlotte Joko Beck's Every Day Zen, which I didn't understand at all.
But then I read about ten more books, and then ten more after that.
And I started coming to sit at the Old Dharma Hall, the one that was upstairs from the stationery store.
And I was lucky.
I came to an Introduction to Zen half-day retreat, and it was led by Zoketsu Norman Fischer.
And I knew I didn't have to look further.
Norman looked at me at one point, and I had never felt seen or understood like that ever before.
I remember thinking afterwards that it was a good thing that he was this wonderful ethical person, because I would probably have followed him anywhere regardless.
I'd found a teacher.
I didn't know it yet, but I'd also found Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Tim can attest to the fact that when I first started with the group, I beat myself black and blue whenever I would make a mistake.
Well, John probably remembers that pretty well too, and Bob, especially if I was doing a job like Tenzo or Doan or Kokyo.
The Doan and Kokyo books that are so great now, that you can just sort of follow the script, were in their infancy.
And change to a service, I remember once at Samish, change to a service.
What happened when Tim scribbled something on a post-it note that Norman had told him to change.
And during kinhin, during our walking meditation, Tim handed this note to me, and then we had service.
Totally screwed it up.
But I realized while working on this talk how much of a parallel there was between the way I reacted to those mistakes and the way I reacted in my life.
Sometimes I did get a message from people of not good enough, and that came from other people, but the message also came from really deep within myself.
Chapter 7, Great Blue Herons.
Apparently it's fairly common that on about the third or fourth day of your first retreat, for a lot of people at least, you just want to be out of there.
You want to be done with it.
You don't care about it.
This was the wrong thing to do.
And I was going to stay for the full retreat because I had said I would, and I keep my commitments.
But I was mentally just gone.

I went outside really early one morning, the next morning, and sat down on this rock that looks out over a lagoon, and there were pink clouds in the sky being reflected in that still water of the lagoon.
And about 80 Great Blue Herons came out of somewhere and flew over the water.
And my mind just stopped.
I don't know if it was for 30 seconds, for two minutes, for an hour, probably more like two minutes.
But I had never had anything like that happen before.
I just wasn't thinking of anything.
I was just present.
I was just fully present.
And the complaining stopped, the mind chatter stopped.
I was just there.
And 16 years later, I still haven't left.
You guys could laugh occasionally.
It's going to be okay.
Chapters 8 and 9, Practice and the Ritual of Letting Go.
When I first started Zen, to me the ritual seemed really beautiful and mysterious.
I could follow along and do what other people were doing, but I didn't really understand what it was about.
You repeat the chants.
You bow when you're told to bow.
But then as I kept participating and as I kept sitting, it seemed like the rituals just sort of soaked in and became a part of me.
It wasn't rote anymore.
Of course, sometimes it is.
But as Norman has pointed out before, that just makes it all the better when it isn't, when you really feel what you're doing.
And so ritual isn't a thing that can be separated out from practice.
Ritual and practice really are the same thing, at least in my mind.
And ritual is a process.
It's not a thing, it's a process.
And it is empty and it is transformative.
There's a koan that points to the nature of ritual.
And I asked him in Dokusan tonight if he remembered this koan, and he thought I might have made it up out of two or three different ones, so I'm not sure if this is right or not.
But a monk asked, what is zazen?
Someone, and I think it might be Zhaozhou, says, non-zazen.
The monk asks, how can zazen be non-zazen?
Zhaozhou replies, because it's alive.
So whether it's zazen or kinhin, and some of you might not know the term zazen, it just means the sitting meditation that we do.
So whether it's zazen or kinhin, the walking meditation, or offering flowers, or chanting, ritual to me is very much alive.
And that's why mistakes don't matter.
And I told Kaylin a couple weeks ago, mistakes don't matter because they're just a part of practice, they're part of that living ritual.
Ritual creates sacred space.
This is not just a room.
And for many years, I could sit in this sacred space and cry and cry and let go, like crying tonight.
I could face the grief that I couldn't really face when I had to be making Nathaniel his dinner, when I had to be taking him to therapy, when I had to be dealing with his meltdowns and loving him.
I couldn't deal with the grief in that real context of the outside world, but I could look at it and be with it and feel it and find some peace with it within the context of our rituals.

Once at Samish, in the real early evening, the light was dimming down in the zendo, and I was sitting on my cushion, and people on both sides of me, and I imagined that if I leaned forward and looked, that line of people would just keep going outside the back of the zendo all the way back to Shakyamuni Buddha.
Unfortunately, I didn't have the courage to lean forward and look, but I think it did do that.
Chapter 10, Out of the Ashes.
In this chapter, Nathaniel continues to play in a rock band.
It's a rock band especially for special needs people, so he continues to play in a rock band.
Last week, he got to play three songs on the big drums.
He was happy, and a couple weeks ago, he got to drive, with just a little help, an enormous humongous John Deere tractor.
The dream of a lifetime, or at least of the last three years.
And the look of shock on his face when that tractor pulled up before he got to go on.
I was expecting just a small tractor, but this salesperson brought out this really big tractor, and the look on Nathaniel's face was one of absolute shock and awe.
I had never seen him look like that ever before, and he still smiles really big when I ask him to talk about the tractor.
Also in this chapter, Connie continues to struggle with chronic, sometimes severe, pain.
Waking up in the night, she is listening to literally hundreds of Dharma talks.
She loves being Eno, but worries that she doesn't have enough energy to do the job well.
One sunny day, she rolls down the windows of her car, puts some Fleetwood Mac on the stereo, and drives down the road, feeling as free and happy as she was when she was 16.
Epilogue.

Sometimes I am present, appreciating a sharp, tangy smell of ozone along the beach, the smell of salt water, or the green smell of red cedar early in the morning when I take my dog out for a walk, or sometimes I'm present watching the hummingbirds that I have enticed to my back deck.
Sometimes, once in a great while, I experience a deep sense of peace, the sound of silence, maybe a brush with emptiness.
But the one thing I really know is I don't really understand any of this, but I'm still here.
So I want to end with a quote, something Norman Fischer said.

*When we sit, we recognize the crucial divine importance of absolutely everything that arises, every thought, every feeling, every breath, every unspeakable, unnameable impulse, but also we recognize the ultimate importance of the others, of the sky, of all the sounds inside and outside the room.
As the mind becomes a little more quiet, the sacredness of everything within and without becomes clear to us.*
I'm going to read that one more time.
I think it's really nice.

*When we sit, we recognize the crucial divine importance of absolutely everything that arises, every thought, every feeling, every breath, every unspeakable, unnameable impulse, but also we recognize the ultimate importance of the others, of the sky, of all the sounds inside and outside the room.
As the mind becomes a little more quiet, the sacredness of everything within and without becomes clear to us.*
This manuscript was respectfully submitted.
Nyogen, Connie, Martin, Energy Source, Pure Emptiness, 824-2006.
How's our time?
Oh, not too bad.
We don't have much time, but any questions or comments?
Sorry?
Oh, there are two different kinds of sign language, but I won't go into that.
Anything else?
Anyone?
**Participant:** Thank you for telling that story, but you must know that Nathaniel is absolutely a product of the love that flows between the two of you.
I've seen him respond to you and you to him.
It's a beautiful job.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** Yeah, it's always bothered me actually when someone, and I'm not referring to you, but when someone says, oh, Connie, you're so good with Nathaniel.
I couldn't do something like that.
How do you do it?
You're so good with them.
Yeah, I didn't want this bloody job.
I had to do it.
Never felt like I had a choice.
**Participant:** Yeah.
You do.
You do.
And you continue to choose.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** I still don't have a choice.
**Participant:** It's a choice of how you deal with what you do.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** I don't think so.
Are you gonna argue with me now?
**Participant:** Connie, I still want to go to Rock Band Night.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** I say what?
**Participant:** I want to go to Rock Band Night.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** Yes.
Out of the Ashes plays on Tuesday nights from 3:30 to 5:30 during the summer there at Boundary Bay.
So stop by and have a beer and enjoy the music.
Tuesdays at 3:30 to 5:30.
And you sing or pick up a tambourine, or there's always a box of percussion instruments for people to play with.
And in that context, it's absolutely unheard of to say something like, oh, I can't sing.
Everyone there can sing.
And I've never seen a happier, more joyous band.
Okay.
That seems like a good note on which to end.
So thank you, everyone.
